results.title: 15 Must-Ride Roller Coasters In 2025 (And The Best Times To Go)
results.description: From record-breaking thrills to legendary wooden rides, here are the top roller coasters in the world and the best times to visit them.
extra_snippets: Whether it’s a traditional wooden coaster that creeks and sways with every turn, or a steel fabricated coaster that offers a smooth ride and complex design, roller coaster enthusiasts by the millions flock to amusement parks each year. About 385 million people ride roller coasters each year at fixed-site amusement parks in North America alone, with over 1.7 billion rides taken.

What is considered the first successful commercial roller coaster made its debut in 1884 at New York's famous Coney Island. Today, there are an estimated 6,600 roller coasters in the world. There isn't a universal preference for wooden or steel roller coasters, as it often comes down to personal preference and the specific ride experience each offers.

Wooden coasters are known for their characteristic swaying and bumpiness along with strong "airtime" moments, while steel coasters generally offer a smoother ride than wooden coasters, and can reach higher speeds and steeper drops. No matter your preference, there’s no denying that roller coasters can being out the little kid in everyone.

results.title: Thrill Ride Therapy: Can Roller Coasters Fight Anxiety?
results.description: Are theme parks the perfect place for immersion and exposure therapy?
extra_snippets: Growing up, Pete Trabucco hated roller coasters. As an adult, he’s ridden more than 1,000 around the world. In fact, he’s grown to love them so much that he wrote the book America’s Top Roller Coasters and Amusement Parks. So, what happened?

Did we conquer all of our fears in two days? Absolutely not! However, it did give us a different outlet for our stress and anxiety. We spend so much time trying to control the outcomes of our lives, but when you’re on a roller coaster, you have to just let go — and that has been an amazing lesson!
Trabucco believes that sense of doom and gloom associated with roller coasters can actually impact other areas of our lives.

Kevin Meyer, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mount Union in Alliance, Ohio, created a unique “Face Your Fear” project for students in his Abnormal Psychology class. To complete the assignment, he took them to Cedar Point Amusement Park, a place best known as “The Roller Coaster Capital of the World.”

The National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) was queried for U.S. emergency department visits from 2004 to 2023 involving neurological injuries sustained on roller coasters in patients under the age of 18 years. Narratives were screened to include only cases with cranial and spinal injuries.

According to the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, approximately 385 million people ride roller coasters each year in North America [1]. These riders are subject to multiple forces, including rapid changes in speed, direction, and gravity, all of which are designed to fall within safety limits.

This study aimed to determine the incidence and types of head, neck, and spine injuries sustained by minors during roller coaster rides with a particular focus on those that may involve neurological structures but also including other musculoskeletal conditions.

results.title: A Thrill Ride - Berkeley Engineering
results.description: Tim Jacobi adores hurtling through the air, whipping around hairpin turns and feeling his stomach do loops. The Berkeley Engineering master's candidate in mechanical engineering is a roller coaster junkie. "It's such a rush, basically," explains Jacobi, who traces his passion to his early teens.
extra_snippets: Tim Jacobi (second from front in bottom row) is part of the brave group testing a prototype of his Eagle amusement park ride, inspired by a childhood toy. The master’s candidate in mechanical engineering, who put his studies on hold in 2004 for a job in the roller-coaster business, now hopes to graduate in December 2008.

Along with his zeal for riding them, Jacobi says roller coasters are “really interesting engineering challenges.” Designing a ride means grappling with such factors as fluids, dynamics, machine design and stress analysis.

Jacobi cut his studies short in 2004 when a dream job opened at S & S. “I decided to jump on it,” he says, hoping eventually to find time to write his thesis and complete one remaining class for his degree. “It was clear that his passion was roller coaster engineering, and we figured out a way to make that dream happen,” says Agogino of her first-ever student specializing in roller coasters.

Jacobi has seen two of his proposals get built—the Huckleberry Splash, a 12-passenger family water plunge, and a 1,200-foot-long roller coaster dubbed the Eagle. The Huckleberry started as a theoretical concept for Jacobi’s thesis. It became reality after S&S CEO Stan Checketts got interested enough to install a mockup in his swimming pool and then construct the ride for a local amusement park.

results.title: 4 Roller Coasters That Put the Theme in Theme Park - The New York Times
results.description: It is a rare roller coaster that tries to give you an experience, not just a scare. Here are a handful that do.
extra_snippets: When roller coasters made their way from Russia to France nearly 200 years ago, they quickly outshone the more routine amusements at park promenades. They are no less central to modern American theme parks, which by definition seek to unify the thrills under a setting or idea (or commercial brand).

As I travel the country visiting theme parks, I think about how true a ride stays to its mission of telling you a story while making your heart leap, and whether it even matters if it does. For some of my favorite coasters, the only point is the thrill. But there is something memorable about a roller coaster with a story.

You see a silhouette of the feared yeti before the coaster continues forward again and back outside, down a steep hill. It’s an exhilarating lurch in and out of the mountain with a more detailed view of the monster before ride’s end. While it isn’t the most intense roller coaster in the world, its attachment to its theme makes it one of the most interesting.

Europe is the overarching theme of the Busch Gardens park in Williamsburg, Va. Inside the Oktoberfest Village section sits an amusing little roller coaster with an element surprising enough to frighten this hard-to-shock enthusiast.

results.title: The Way We Live Now: 6-20-99: The Science of: Roller Coasters; High Rollers - The New York Times
results.description: New generation of roller coasters uses advances technological advances to enhance speed and thrills; listing of the top five coasters among connoisseurs; photo (L)
extra_snippets: Roller coasters have been around for more than 100 years, but for most of that time, they've been in a state of arrested development. In fact, it's only recently that ride technology has advanced much beyond the principles of the first roller coaster, Gravity Pleasure, on Coney Island, which opened in 1884.

Next year, the 80-mile-an-hour Son of Beast, the first all-wood coaster to include a 360-degree loop, will open at Kings Island, in Ohio. ... The most extreme roller coasters -- those that send their passengers zooming along extravagantly curlicued routes, at speeds that would be illegal on any highway -- require structures made of steel.

But using computers capable of making very precise calculations, designers determined that building the loop in a teardrop shape would distribute the force more gently and make the experience much smoother. The resulting coaster, Revolution, in Valencia, Calif., was so immensely popular that competitors eager to duplicate its success embarked on what Paul Ruben, the publisher of Park World magazine, calls ''a roller-coaster arms race.''

Stories of roller-coaster tragedies are the stuff of legend. In reality, there have been only 42 such deaths in the last 11 years. Nearly all have been flukes: in one case, someone ducked under a track to retrieve his hat, at which point an oncoming coaster collided with his head.

extra_snippets: Technology plays starring but seldom-seen role in operations of roller coasters; machines, not people, insure that cars whiz down the track at right speed, do not collide and do not hit obstacles that block route; Six Flags Magic Mountain amusement park in Valencia, Calif, has Riddler's Revenge, billed as nation's fastest and tallest stand-up roller coaster; ride operator secures automatic safety bars, but rest of work is done by two Allen-Bradley PLC-5's, which serve as brains of massive control system built primarily by Rockwell International's Allen-Bradley unit; they provide full set of instructions every 20 to 40 milliseconds to massive control system built around them; manufacturers prefer to describe innards of theme ride technology as 'programmable logic controllers' rather than as computers; photos (M)

From the safety announcements played as passengers wait to get on board to the photographs of screaming riders sold at the exit, technology plays a starring but seldom-seen role in the operations of roller coasters.

Indeed, on the Riddler's Revenge, billed as the nation's fastest and tallest stand-up roller coaster, the job of a ride operator is similar to that of a flight attendant: make sure that the automatic safety bars are secure and that stuffed animals are stowed away.
